topicName: Data Structures and Memory Encoding (Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Data Structures and Memory Encoding in Redis"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis is much more than a simple key-value store. It is an in-memory data structure store that supports various data types. Understanding how Redis encodes these types in memory is crucial for optimizing performance, scaling applications, and managing RAM consumption."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Strings: The Foundation and IntEncoding"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The String is the most basic Redis data type, but it is binary safe, meaning it can contain any data, such as a JPEG image or a serialized Ruby object. Internally, Redis strings are represented by the Simple Dynamic String (SDS) implementation."},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"Depending on the value, Redis chooses different internal encodings for Strings:"},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"int: Used when a string value can be represented as a 64-bit signed integer. Redis shares integers from 0 to 9999 to save memory."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"embstr: Used for short strings (typically less than 44 bytes). It allocates memory for the SDS structure and the object header in a single contiguous chunk."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"raw: Used for longer strings. Allocates the SDS structure and the header separately."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"SET counter 100
OBJECT ENCODING counter
# Output: "int"

SET greeting "Hello"
OBJECT ENCODING greeting
# Output: "embstr""},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Hashes: Maps of Fields and Values"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis Hashes are maps between string fields and string values, making them perfect for representing objects (e.g., a user profile with fields like name, age, and email)."},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Hashes are encoded using:"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ziplist: The default for small hashes. It stores fields and values consecutively in a compact memory layout to minimize pointer overhead."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"hashtable: Used when the hash exceeds the configuration limits (hash-max-ziplist-entries or hash-max-ziplist-value), providing O(1) lookups."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"HSET user:1000 name "Alice" age "30"
OBJECT ENCODING user:1000
# Output: "ziplist" or "listpack" in newer versions"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Lists: Ordered Collections"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis Lists are simply lists of strings, sorted by insertion order. You can add elements to the head (left) or the tail (right) of a list. They are heavily used for message queues and task lists."},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Historically, lists were encoded using linked lists or ziplists. Modern Redis versions utilize 'quicklist', which is a hybrid data structure: a doubly linked list of ziplists (or listpacks). This balances memory efficiency with fast insertion and deletion."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"LPUSH tasks "task1"
RPUSH tasks "task2"
OBJECT ENCODING tasks
# Output: "quicklist""},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Sets: Unordered Unique Collections"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis Sets are unordered collections of unique strings. They support powerful operations like unions, intersections, and differences."},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Encodings for Sets:"},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"intset: Used when all elements of the set are integers and the total number of elements is below a specific threshold (set-max-intset-entries)."},{"order":24,"type":"bullet_point","text":"hashtable: Used for larger sets or sets containing non-integer strings."},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"SADD tags "redis" "database" "nosql"
OBJECT ENCODING tags
# Output: "hashtable""},{"order":26,"type":"subheading","text":"5. Sorted Sets (ZSets): Ordered by Score"},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"Sorted Sets are similar to Sets, but every member is associated with a score. Elements are always ordered by their score, allowing for rapid range queries."},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Sorted Sets use a dual-encoding structure to maintain performance and order:"},{"order":29,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ziplist (or listpack): Used for small sorted sets, storing elements sequentially."},{"order":30,"type":"bullet_point","text":"skiplist + hashtable: Used for larger sorted sets. A hashtable maps members to scores for O(1) lookups, while a skip list maintains order for efficient range queries."},{"order":31,"type":"code","text":"ZADD leaderboard 1500 "PlayerA" 2000 "PlayerB"
OBJECT ENCODING leaderboard
# Output: "ziplist" (or "skiplist")"},{"order":32,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":33,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis dynamically transitions between memory encodings based on data size and type. By tuning configuration parameters like max-ziplist-entries, developers can find the optimal balance between CPU overhead and RAM consumption for their specific workloads."}]
